title: Why farmers fill tractor tyres with beet juice

lines.text: Why is this farmer pumping vegetable juice into his tractor tyres?
A tractor needs heavy back wheels. Too light, and they spin in the mud, or the whole thing tips up when it lifts a bale.
So farmers fill the tyres about three quarters full of liquid.
Water is cheap. But in winter, it freezes solid.
So they added salt, calcium chloride. It stops the freezing, but it eats the steel wheels from the inside.
Then someone tried the leftovers from sugar factories.
Sugar beet juice. It's heavier than water, it doesn't freeze until about minus thirty seven, and it's gentle on steel.
So the heaviest part of that tractor is, technically, a vegetable.
Comment what you want to know next.

experiment.hypothesis: First Short in george's approved vivid look (Neutral tone mapping, saturated grade, pill-bodied character). An everyday object with a weird secret plus a useful 'why' arc.
experiment.fish: #600 (In Canada, tractor tires are filled up with vegetable juice)

facts.claim: Liquid ballast is added to tractor rear tyres for weight; fill only to about 75%; never plain water (it freezes).
Calcium chloride stops the water freezing but is very corrosive; steel wheels corrode without tubes.
Beet juice ballast (Rim Guard) is a sugar beet processing by-product, about 10.7-11 lb per US gallon (water 8.3), freeze-resistant to about -35 F (-37 C), and sold as non-corrosive and non-toxic.

experiment.notes: Freeze point and non-corrosive claims are the maker's; script says 'about' and 'gentle on steel' rather than 'never rusts'. Tyre-tipping with a loaded front loader is why rear ballast is used (manuals).
